t.6.6.1: Having seen the terrible, fear-inspiring deed done in Laṅkā by the great-souled Hanumān, as if by Śakra himself, the lord of the rākṣasas, his face somewhat lowered in shame, spoke to all the rākṣasas.
t.6.6.2: The city of Laṅkā, so hard to withstand, has been both entered and violated by that mere monkey, and Sītā, daughter of Janaka, has been seen by him.
t.6.6.3: The palace, the sacred sanctuary, was violated, the foremost rākṣasas were slain, and the whole city of Laṅkā was thrown into turmoil by Hanumān.
t.6.6.5: The noble and wise declare that victory has counsel as its root; therefore, O mighty ones, I desire counsel concerning Rāma.
t.6.6.4: What shall I do? May good fortune be yours! Or what is fitting to be done next? Let us be told what is effective, and what, once done, would be well done.
t.6.6.6: In this world there are three kinds of men: the best, the lowest, and the middling. Of these, when they are gathered together, I shall now tell the merits and faults.
t.6.6.7: With ministers devoted to one's welfare and capable in deciding matters of counsel, or with friends who share a common purpose, or else with kinsmen who wish one well.
t.6.6.8: He who, together with others, first takes counsel and then sets his undertakings in motion, and who also makes effort in matters that rest with fate, him they call the best of men.
t.6.6.9: He who ponders a matter alone, sets his mind on dharma alone, and carries out his undertakings alone, him they call a middling man.
t.6.6.10: He who, without weighing the merits and faults, abandons reliance on fate and, saying "I shall do it," neglects the task at hand, is the lowest of men.
t.6.6.11: Just as these men are always of the best, the worst, and the middling kind, so too counsel should be understood as being of the best, the worst, and the middling kind.
t.6.6.12: Where the ministers, having reached unanimity by an eye guided by the treatises, have cast aside all doubts, that is called the best counsel.
t.6.6.13: When the ministers, though holding many differing opinions while deciding a matter, come back to agreement, that counsel, having reached unanimity, is considered the middling kind.
t.6.6.15: Therefore, you best of counsellors, let your honours settle upon a well-deliberated, sound course of action; this is the thing most needful for me to do.
t.6.6.14: Where the counsellors, each taking a stand on his own opinion against the other's, argue back and forth, and no good is found even in agreement, that counsel is called the lowest.
t.6.6.17: And clearly Rāghava, together with his younger brother and followed by his army, will easily cross the ocean with fitting speed and vigor.
t.6.6.16: For Rāma, surrounded by thousands of heroic monkeys, is advancing on the city of Laṅkā to lay siege to us.
t.6.6.18: Now that this affair has come to such a pass, with hostilities against the monkeys, let everything that is beneficial for my city and my army be deliberated upon.
